q: The discovery of the electron in 1897 prompted J.J. Thomson (1856 - 1940) to suggest a model of the ____.
e: J.J. Thomson proposed the first major structural model of the atom following his discovery of the electron.

q: He suggested that an atom might be a spherical volume of positive charge with electrons embedded inside it like currant in a bun (or) plums in a ____.
e: Thomson's model is famously known as the plum pudding model due to its analogy of electrons scattered within a sphere of positive charge.

q: For this reason, Thomson's model is called the plum pudding model of the ____.
e: The plum pudding model was the prevailing atomic model before Rutherford's gold foil experiment disproved it.

q: Under the supervision of Ernest Rutherford (1871-1937), Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden performed an important experiment in ____.
e: The famous gold foil experiment, conducted by Geiger and Marsden under Rutherford, was performed in 1911.

q: In this experiment, a thin metal foil was bombarded with a beam of positively charged ____ particles.
e: Rutherford's experiment used alpha particles, which are helium nuclei, to probe the structure of the atom.

q: Most of the alpha particles passed straight through the foil, but a few were deflected from their original direction through very large ____.
e: The unexpected large-angle deflection of some alpha particles indicated the presence of a dense, positively charged core in the atom.

q: Such large deflections were completely unexpected on the basis of Thomson's model, in which positive charges are evenly distributed throughout the ____.
e: Thomson's model predicted only minor deflections because the positive charge was thought to be spread diffusely throughout the atom.

q: On the basis of his observation, Rutherford concluded that the atom must be largely empty space with all of its positive charges and most of its mass concentrated in a small ____.
e: Rutherford deduced that the atom's mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny central region, which he named the nucleus.

q: This concentrated volume at the centre of the atom is called the ____.
e: The nucleus is the dense, positively charged central core of an atom, containing nearly all of its mass.

q: Negatively charged electrons are moving around the tiny ____.
e: In Rutherford's model, electrons orbit the central nucleus, similar to planets orbiting the sun.

q: In 1913, Niels Bohr (1885 - 1962), a Danish Physicist, proposed a new model of the atom by applying the ____ theory.
e: Niels Bohr incorporated quantum theory into the atomic model to resolve the stability issues of Rutherford's model.

q: In Bohr's model, the electrons move in circular orbits around the ____.
e: Bohr's model depicts electrons traveling in specific, quantized circular orbits around the atomic nucleus.

q: The electric force between the positively charged proton inside the nucleus and the negatively charged electron holds the electron in ____.
e: The Coulomb attractive force between the positive nucleus and negative electron provides the centripetal force required to keep the electron in orbit.

q: However, only certain orbits are allowed in this ____.
e: Bohr postulated that electrons can only occupy specific, quantized orbits with fixed energies.

q: The electron is never found between the allowed ____.
e: Electrons cannot exist in the space between quantized orbits; they can only transition instantaneously between them.

q: However it can jump from one orbit to ____.
e: Electrons can transition between allowed orbits by absorbing or emitting a photon with energy equal to the difference between the orbits.

q: Bohr assumed that the atom does not emit energy in the form of radiation when the electron is in an allowed ____.
e: Bohr's stationary state postulate states that an electron in an allowed orbit does not radiate energy, ensuring atomic stability.

q: Hence the total energy of the atom remains constant and it resolved the instability of the atom which is a difficulty of the ____ model.
e: Classical electromagnetism predicted that an orbiting electron in Rutherford's model would continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, which Bohr's model resolved.
